michigan.headline: Michigan 18, UCLA 16
michigan.body:
Michigan 18, UCLA 16

Alex.Drain
November 21st, 2026 at 8:38 PM

For the first time since 2020, and the first time since the "two point derby" rules were instituted, Michigan Football played a game that went to triple overtime. This one was another grindingly dull defensive struggle, with neither team able to cobble together offensive success for long. Michigan never trailed, but failed to close it out in regulation and then needed a heroic kick from a young kicker to save themselves in 2OT, before a key injury to UCLA's QB Ty Dieffenbach gave the Wolverines a leg up to win in the third extra period. The Wolverines upset the nation's #4 team today, 18-16, qualifying for a bowl game, but what we witnessed did not meaningfully change what we know about this team.
Michigan received the opening kickoff and their first drive started promisingly. Savion Hiter ripped off a 24 yard run, one of the few explosive runs that the Bruins' vaunted defense has allowed this season. His second carry was also positive, a 5 yard gain and Michigan was feeling confident about their run game. Unfortunately, their pass game couldn't match. A Bryce Underwood rollout found no one open and led to a small scramble out of bounds to set up 3rd & 2. On that down, Underwood looked deep for Travis Johnson, who was well covered and the ball was a bit overthrown anyway. Curiously, facing 4th & 2 on the +46, Kyle Whittingham opted to punt. Cam Brown landed UCLA on their own 8 with the punt.
The Michigan defense took advantage of the field position with a quick three-and-out. Ty Dieffenbach threw behind his intended receiver on first down, followed by a productive run up the gut by RB Wayne Knight, a play that ended with Rod Moore delivering a thundering hit on Knight short of the sticks. UCLA was faced with the same 3rd & 2 that Michigan had just failed on and Michigan's defense was ready for the checkdown to Knight in the flat, as multiple Wolverines were there to knock him out of bounds before reaching the first down line.

[Bryan Fuller]
The home team got the ball back around midfield and went back to feeding Hiter. He ran on first down for eight solid yards and Underwood looked for Travis Johnson on a backshoulder throw on 2nd down, which saw CB Rodrick Pleasant yank Johnson in the jersey. No flag, incomplete. Now back in that same 3rd & 2, Savion Hiter was stopped dead in his tracks for no gain. This time on 4th & 2 Whittingham rolled the dice to go for it, with Michigan calling straight QB power for Underwood. There was no room to run, as UCLA's defensive front blew up the blocking and Underwood was hit in the backfield, never coming close to gaining the first down.
So, it was a turnover on downs and UCLA got the ball just inside their half of midfield and went to work. A pair of Dieffenbach keepers (one should've been given on a read option) got UCLA to, guess what, 3rd & 2. This time someone finally converted... due to a penalty. Michigan sent a blitz, which was in the neutral zone pre-snap, creating a free play for the Bruins. The play saw Dieffenbach complete a pass to Brian Rowe Jr., who then turned upfield and fumbled. Michigan got on the loose ball, but the play didn't matter due to the pre-snap penalty. First down UCLA.
After gaining their first fresh set of downs of the game, nothing much changed for the skittish UCLA offense. The Bruins dialed up a screen that looked well up but the skittish Dieffenbach threw the ball high and incomplete. Then, after a six yard run, Dieffenbach made an ill-advised throw on 3rd & 4 that was intercepted by Chris Bracy at the Michigan 11. Dieffenbach stared down his receiver and failed to see Bracy peeling off his receiver to snag the ball. Through two drives, UCLA's QB looked very uncomfortable and the Michigan defense was winning this battle so far.
The turnover deep in territory gave Michigan's offense rather unfavorable field position, but they cobbled together the best drive of the game to that point. The key early plays were an Underwood scramble that gained 15 yards and a pass by Underwood to Mason Bonner that tacked on 15 more. Michigan was now out closer to midfield and continued to gain yardage on productive plays. An Underwood keeper picked up 8 and then the Michigan QB hooked up with Channing Goodwin over the middle for another first down. For the first time all game, Michigan was approaching scoring position.
[AFTER THE JUMP: did they score?]

[Fuller]
Just as things were looking up, they began to turn south. Underwood threw behind an open Travis Johnson on first down, which was followed by a swing pass to Hiter for a few. On 3rd & 6, Underwood was pressured and threw incomplete, but the referees ruled that UCLA LB Trent Hendrick was lined up offisde. The free five yards gave Michigan a mulligan, one they would squander spectacularly. On 3rd & 1, Michigan attempted to have Hiter rush it for a first down but he was met by two linebackers in the backfield for a TFL. Now on 4th & ~2.5, Underwood felt pressure again but was able to find Salesi Moa open. The pass was a bit behind Moa but was catchable. Problem is, Moa dropped it. The second turnover on downs of the game for the Wolverines.
UCLA's offense was still stuck in a bit of a rut. They gained one first down after three consecutive run plays ended with Dieffenbach surging ahead on a 3rd & short for first down. But that was all they could muster. The pass game was still unproductive for the Bruins, as Dieffenbach threw an incompletion on first down and scrambled short of the sticks on the next third down. Faced with a 4th & short from the +46, Bob Chesney opted to play field position and his punter rewarded him. Curtis Gerrand delivered a 45 yard boot to pin Michigan on the 1.
The Wolverine offense was clearly superior to the Bruin offense at this stage of the game, even if it wasn't leading to points. Their next drive would gain 53 yards over 11 plays but wouldn't change the goose egg on the scoreboard. The key plays on this one were a catch-and-run by Travis Johnson after breaking a tackle and a completion to Mason Bonner down the seam for 26 yards on 3rd & 8. The throw by Underwood wasn't great but Bonner wrestled it away from Pleasant. Michigan gained one more first down after that, picked up by Underwood on the ground as Michigan approached scoring range.

[Fuller]
It was the ability of the UCLA defense to create big negative plays, their signature trait this season, that got them off the field. Underwood was pressured on the next play and he couldn't outrun this one, eventually being brought down by a gang-sack of Darold DeNgohe, Sammy Omosigho, and Scott Taylor. That was a devastating loss of nine yards meaning that after a run into a light box on 2nd down, Michigan was still faced with the predicament of a 3rd & 14. Pressure came on Underwood again and his throw for Travis Johnson was way too high and deep (Johnson wasn't really open either). As Michigan punted, some began to remark that all four Michigan drives of the game to that point had reached UCLA territory, yet they had culminated in zero points.
UCLA's defense was continuing to let their offense off the hook but that offense continued to scuffle. The Bruins found one thing that worked on their next drive, an RPO slant to Aidan Mizell, which they ran on two consecutive plays for first downs, with tempo in between. They actually tried to do it a third time, but that one was thrown behind the receiver and broken up by Jyaire Hill. After an unproductive run, Dieffenbach was asked to complete a pass in a 3rd & long situation but wouldn't have the time to do so, as Enow Etta and Dominic Nichols arrived to sack him.
So, the Bruins were forced to punt again and this one was a dud, a line drive that allowed Salesi Moa to rip off a 23 yard return. Michigan's next drive would begin in Bruin territory, their fifth time in five drives that they began in plus territory. This drive would actually be one of Michigan's worst of the game, but because it started in such advantageous field position, it finally ended in points. The only notable play was an Underwood strike to Deakon Tonielli (passes to the TE?? wow!!) because otherwise UCLA had Michigan bottled up, tackling two rush plays for a loss and making a prompt tackle when Michigan waved the white flag on 3rd down. Jacob Baggett was asked to attempt a 46 yard FG and the freshman drilled it, his first collegiate field goal make. 3-0 Michigan.

[Patrick Barron]
There were now fewer than 4 minutes remaining in the first half as UCLA's offense took the field again. What unfolded over that stretch was a sequence of events defined by two strip sack fumbles. First there was one that happened to UCLA, occurring after they had gained a pair of first downs. The Bruins had gotten out to the Michigan 46 before Chase Taylor's blitz sacked Dieffenbach, which was followed on the next play by a John Henry Daley pass rush that hit Dieffenbach as he was throwing, producing a loose ball that was recovered by Dom Nichols.
Michigan was energized and now had a chance for additional points with 44 seconds remaining. But on just the second play of the drive it was UCLA's turn to return the favor, as a pass rush by Aiden Gobaira around Evan Link hit Underwood just before he began to throw, producing a fumble that Gobaiara himself recovered. It was ruled an incomplete pass on the field but the replay booth correctly overturned it to a fumble. UCLA ball on their own 45, with 32 seconds on the clock.
The visitors needed to work quickly here and they did. Despite a holding call on first down, Dieffenbach would have consecutive completions to Brian Rowe Jr. and Semaj Morgan for solid gains to advance UCLA to field goal range. Though kicker Mateen Bhagani has struggled on distance kicks this season, he had little difficulty fitting a 44 yard field goal between the uprights on the last play of the first half to knot the score. At halftime, the teams were tied 3-3.
The first drive of the second half for UCLA did not indicate anything new or a breakthrough of success for the Bruins on offense. They gained a first down when Anthony Woods rushed for five yards on 3rd & 4, catching the defense off-guard. But then John Henry Daley came to the rescue, making a shoestring sack of Dieffenbach and then tackling a Knight run for a loss (along with his friends). That set up 3rd & long and a throw to Semaj Morgan on a mesh route was not enough to move the chains. Another punt, pinning Michigan on the 10.

[Fuller]
Likewise, the first Michigan drive was more of the same: solid ball movement into UCLA territory before everything comes screeching to a halt. The two key plays were an Underwood rollout and completion to Salesi Moa that gained 13 yards, as well as a Savion Hiter run for 14 yards out to midfield. What followed was bizarre playcalling, culminating in a 3rd & 8 in which Michigan asked Underwood to run the ball (why?) and there was no blocking in front of him. UCLA made a quick tackle and Michigan punted the ball. The same as ever.
The same script seemed to be unfolding as UCLA quickly went first-down-and-out. One completion to Landon Ellis moved the sticks but more Michigan pressure thanks to their suffocating dominance at the line of scrimmage put the special teams units on the field. Little did we know, Bob Chesney was about to roll the dice in the ballsiest way, attempting a fake punt on 4th & 7 from his own 27. The play call snapped the ball to the upback Anthony Sacca, who had one man to beat to get the first down. That would be special teamer Nico Andrighetto, who was juked by Sacca and from there, Sacca was off to the races. He gained 27 yards, UCLA's longest gain of the day, and gave his offense new life with a fresh set of downs at the +46.
Yet the Bruins couldn't do anything with it. Humorously, the first play after the momentum-swinging fake punt was a cold splash of reality to the face. They tried a pitch play to Wayne Knight, who was hit for a loss of 2. Then Dieffenbach delivered a bad ball for an open Semaj Morgan. The QB bounced back a bit with a nice pass to Aidan Mizell on a crosser to set up a 4th & short situation, which the Bruins obviously went for. UCLA asked Dieffenbach to rush for the first down but he would be hit just before he reached the line to gain, stopped on his tracks by Troy Bowles and Nathaniel Staehling. Turnover on downs, Michigan ball.

[Fuller]
In the same way that UCLA was unable to capitalize on the momentum from their fake punt, Michigan couldn't capitalize on the good vibes from making this big fourth down stop. Rather than putting together a strong drive to take the lead, they went three-and-out, with two Bryce Underwood completions sandwiched around a three yard run. Michigan punted again and this trench warfare style battle continued.
The moment that changed the feel of the game came on the first play of UCLA's next drive, when the Michigan defense forced another turnover. Or, I should say, took advantage of a turnover. The Wolverines didn't do much to make the game-changing play, as Ty Dieffenbach pulled the trigger to throw but may have squeezed the ball too tightly. The pigskin squibbed out of his hand, coming free before his arm was coming forward and the ball ended up on the turf. Trey Pierce landed on it at the UCLA 15 and Michigan's offense was given the huge break they needed.
Michigan was determined to cash it in on the ground. Two Savion Hiter runs gained a first down, one of which seeing the young back impressively break tackles. Things went backwards from there, as Hiter's Wildcat was stuffed and then his second down carry was tackled for a loss. Forced to throw the football on 3rd & Goal from the 7, Underwood punted it up for the breakout star of the game, TE Mason Bonner. The big guy went up and brought the ball in, bobbling it for a few steps but he managed to secure it before exiting the end zone. The game's first touchdown, coming with 13 minutes remaining in the game. 10-3 Michigan.
If you thought that seeing a Michigan touchdown might snap the UCLA offense into a better form, you would have been wrong. They did gain a couple of first downs on the next drive but self-inflected wounds did them in. This time it wasn't Dieffenbach who was to blame but his receivers. The play was 3rd & 15 from the UCLA 44, Dieffenbach rolled out and found Landon Ellis open down the sideline in front of a pair of Michigan defenders. Dieffenbach delivered an excellent ball that hit him in the numbers but Ellis dropped it. Drive over and UCLA punted again.

[Fuller]
Time was now starting to be an issue for UCLA. The clock now read 9:10 in the 4th quarter as Michigan began their next drive. Kyle Whittingham's team needed to begin bleeding the clock in this game but they would only be able to salt 3:46 away on this drive. Two first downs were obtained, one from a Hiter toss play and one via penalty, as referees called Ta'Shawn James for a defensive pass interference after he got tangled up with Mason Bonner. Things ended there, as the Bruins clamped down against the run and Underwood's attempt to scramble was brought down for a loss of -1 on 3rd down. Michigan punted again.
The Bruins had the ball back, starting this drive on their own 23, with 5:24 to go. They gained a first down on a clever slip screen to Knight and then followed that up with a nine yard Knight run. From there, things unraveled, as Josh Phifer was called for a false start and then back to abck UCLA runs were stopped. Now faced with 4th & 6 from his own 38 with 2:30 remaining and two timeouts, Bob Chesney kept the offense on the field rather than punt. However, he would burn one of those timeouts to set it up, making the play that followed for (more or less) all the marbles. Jay Hill ramped up his blitzing and sent the house, but Dieffenbach stood in and delivered a good ball to Semaj Morgan on an out route to gain a first down.
UCLA was still alive. It didn't look like they'd survive much longer as they continued to struggle to crack the Michigan defense, setting up a 3rd & 9 from midfield that was the big play of the sequence. This was a quick flip by Dieffenbach out to Knight, who managed to bounce off the tackle of Smith Snowden and continue going upfield where he broke a tackle from Troy Bowles and got the first down. It was immensely deflating to Michigan partisans watching, followed up by another "oof" play as Dieffenbach completed a jump ball to Leland Smith down the sideline, bringing it in despite double coverage.

[Fuller]
The Bruins were up to the 14, their first red zone trip of the day. UCLA was limited in play calling by having just one timeout remaining as the clock ticked under one minute to go, but they were content to let Javian Thomas to run it twice. The second of these gained a first down, crucially stopping the clock and allowing UCLA to run it once more before burning that timeout. Once that occurred, it was 2nd & Goal from the 1.5 yard line with 17 seconds remaining. The Bruins now decided to pass it and looked for Semaj Morgan in the end zone. There was a window, but the ball was too high.
Now on 3rd & Goal, UCLA put Anthony Woods in the Wildcat, who rushed towards the line of scrimmage before leaping up and floating a pop pass over the dogpile in front of him to TE Brayden Loftin, who was breaking open in the end zone. Touchdown Bruins, with 10 seconds left to play. Some wondered if Chesney might go for 2, but he opted to kick the extra point, tying the game at 10. Michigan got the ball one last time and decided to run another fake kneel down for whatever reason, which ended the half to the enjoyment of whoever finds that play amusing.
So, for the second time this season, a miserable Michigan home game with little offense that the Wolverines should have won in regulation was headed to overtime. As in the Indiana game, the opposition would start with the ball in OT after Michigan won the coin toss. But unlike the IU game, the opposition didn't quickly score a touchdown. Instead, the play would be halted after the first play, when Dieffenbach rushed for a six yard gain and was tackled, causing an injury. Dieffenbach stayed down in immense pain after the tackle and medical support was called. After multiple minutes on the ground, UCLA's backup QB was carted off.

The other Iamaleava [Barron]
With Dieffenbach out of the picture, Madden Iamaleava subbed into the game, the younger brother of the QB who Dieffenbach replaced earlier in the season (Nico). Iamaleava had some game experience, having played during an earlier Dieffenbach injury against Illinois last week. To ease him in, the UCLA coaches dialed up a run for Knight, which Michigan expected and stopped. Now in a 3rd & 5 situation Iamaleava was asked to throw and had Semaj Morgan open over the middle. The throw was too far in front and Morgan couldn't bring it in. Chesney sent Bhagani out and he connected on a 38 yard FG, tucking it inside the right upright. 13-10 Bruins.
Next was Michigan's turn on offense, which nearly turned disastrous as a miscommunication between Underwood and Travis Johnson led to an errant pass that Scooter Jackson was nearly able to intercept. Michigan dodged a bullet there and then those two righted the wrong with a first down pass on a slant to get Michigan inside the 15. Underwood rushed on the next play, gaining four yards before going out of bounds. A negative run followed, as Hiter was dropped for a loss by Gobaira, forcing Michigan to throw it on third down. Underwood looked for Johnson again but this pass was too hot and too far in front of him. Jacob Baggett went out and made a 29 yard FG to send the game to 2OT tied at 13.
Possession order is inverted in 2OT, so Michigan went right back out on offense. This series left a lot to be desired, as Bryce Underwood sacked himself for a brutal loss of nine yards on first down and two incompletions followed. This left Jacob Baggett in a dicey situation, but the young kicker proved a hero by making a 52 yard FG to give Michigan a 16-13 lead and stave off a likely loss. The pressure was now back on UCLA.
Little did we know but the game was essentially over. Madden Iamaleava was not good enough to give the Bruins what they needed, tripping over himself on a 2nd & 4 carry for a loss of 3, which was followed by a mind-boggling play. Iamaleava rolled out of the pocket and had a huge swath of green grass in front of him to run for the first down and then some. He also had a tight end breaking open for a first down underneath if he wanted a slightly harder play. Instead, Iamaleava's eyes were solely on the end zone. He failed to see either option until ti was too late, as Troy Bowles finally caught up to bring Iamaleava down by the time he decided to scramble. This forced UCLA's kicker to answer and Bhagani obliged, hitting a 38 yarder to send the game to 3OT.

[Barron]
Under current college football rules, the two teams alternate two point tries per "inning" until the tie is broken. UCLA was up first and Iamaleava remained incompetent. He received some protection on his try but continued to look painfully uncomfortable, unable to spot anything in the end zone and running directly into the Michigan defensive line. Michigan now had a chance to win and they had the better quarterback at this juncture. The play call from Jim Harding was a rollout to the right, Underwood's signature skill. Bryce saw Jalen Hoffman open in the end zone and launched a pass just over the outstretched arms of the defender. Hoffman caught it and that was it. 2-point try successful and Michigan won, 18-16.
The box score slightly favors UCLA in terms of total yardage, 296-247, and on a YPP basis, 4.0-3.7. Neither team was able to run it much, Michigan mustering 3.7 YPC and UCLA mustering 3.5 YPC after the sacks were excluded (both teams were sacked four times for similar yardage). UCLA's passing game was marginally more prolific, but the Dieffenbach self-fumble looms large as a particularly crushing moment that swung the game against the Bruins on a passing play. Indeed, UCLA turned it over 3 times to just 1 for Michigan, one of the rare games where Michigan has won the turnover battle this season.
On an individual level, Underwood was 11/24 for 127 yards, 1 touchdown and 0 interceptions. Dieffenbach was 19/30 for 188 yards, 0 touchdowns and 1 interception. Both QBs lost a strip sack fumble, while Dieffenbach had the other fumble. Savion Hiter had 104 yards on 26 carries, his first career 100+ yard game. Knight, in contrast, had 30 yards on 11 carries. For the Michigan passing game, this will be remembered as the "Tight End Game", as Mason Bonner led the way with three catches for 47 yards and a touchdown and Hoffman reeled in the game winner (Deakon Tonielli had a catch for 17 yards). Why it took Michigan's staff 11 games to realize they had viable tight ends, I don't know.

[Barron]
With the win, Michigan is now 6-5 on the season. They will have the ability to go to a bowl game, if they should accept such an invite, and today is the team's fourth victory by one score (they also have three defeats by one score). The general consensus before this game was that Kyle Whittingham would be looking for another job and I don't think anything today will change the opinion of that from most Michigan fans. Michigan's excellent defense remains good enough to produce a win today against an offense that is not as good as they seemed, but the Wolverines didn't show us anything today that we didn't already know. How the university's new leadership feels remains to be seen.
There is one more game to go in the regular season. Next week will be the first meeting of Ohio State and Michigan in which both teams have 4+ losses at the time of the game since 1966 (the only other instance was 1959). The Buckeyes succumbed today to Nebraska, officially knocking the out of the CFP picture and causing more Ohio State fans to call for the firing of Ryan Day. How. much the Scarlet & Gray will have in the tank will determine who wins next weekend, because I doubt that Michigan will do anything beyond what wev'e seen from them this season. That game will kickoff at noon on Saturday and will be broadcast on Tubi FOX.

michigan.headline: Position grades from Michigan’s  overtime win over UCLA
michigan.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 21: Savion Hiter #5 of the Michigan Wolverines runs the ball during the first quarter against Malik Hartford #12 of the UCLA Bruins at Michigan Stadium on November 21, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Jaime Crawford/Getty Images) | Getty Images

It took a while, but Michigan pulled off the upset on Saturday and took down undefeated UCLA in overtime at the Big House by a final score of 18-16. It wasn’t perfect across the board, but here’s a look at the position grades from the win.

Quarterback – C-

Bryce Underwood made his first start for Michigan since he was benched against Penn State all the way back in Week 7. He didn’t look good last week against Oregon, but showed some improvement this week against UCLA, completing 11-of-24 passes for 127 yards and one touchdown. He also did have a fumble right before halftime, stalling out Michigan’s drive near midfield.

Underwood didn’t do a great job throwing the ball downfield, overthrowing Travis Johnson on multiple occasions, but did look a bit more comfortable in the short-to-intermediate game, hitting the tight ends for some nice chunk plays. He saved his best throw for last, hitting Jalen Hoffman in the flat for the two-point conversion to win the game. He’ll likely start again next week, and probably gives Michigan the best chance to beat Ohio State.

MICHIGAN UPSETS NO. 4 UCLA IN A 3 OT THRILLER

(via CBS) pic.twitter.com/XSqVbUEFg5
— FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) November 22, 2026

Running Back – B+

For the second straight week, Savion Hiter was Michigan’s lead ball-carrier, and he got an overwhelming amount of the work among the running backs. He finished the game with 26 carries for 104 yards. Bryson Kuzdzal chipped in with four carries for 11 yards.

UCLA boasts one of the best defenses in the country, and you could tell, with Hiter running it into plenty of brick walls throughout the game. He still was able to show some burst and physicality, though, with runs of 24 and 14 yards, helping him get over 100 yards for a second straight week. It was a solid but unspectacular day for Michigan’s freshman, who will hopefully play a big role next week against the Buckeyes.

Wide Receiver – C-

Michigan was without JJ Buchanan and Andrew Marsh in this game, meaning the freshmen Travis Johnson and Salesi Moa were relied on as the top options in the passing game. Neither one did anything particularly impressive, with Johnson hauling in three passes for 32 yards and Moa having two receptions for 18 yards. Moa also did have a costly drop on fourth down, which ended a first-quarter drive in UCLA territory.

Travis Johnson did have an opportunity for a few big plays on the sideline, but was overthrown twice and had a pass interference not called against him in the first quarter. Look for him to be involved next week, even without great results on Saturday.

Tight End – A+

It only took eleven games and the two top wide receivers not playing, but Michigan’s tight ends were finally featured in the game plan this week. And they were really good – so good it makes you wonder why they weren’t being featured much earlier in the year.

The best of the bunch was freshman Mason Bonner, who showed some good chemistry with Underwood and hauled in three passes for 47 yards and his first career touchdown – an impressive contested catch in the corner of the end zone to give Michigan the lead in the fourth quarter. Jalen Hoffman also had the biggest play of the day, catching the two-point conversion for the victory – his only reception of the game.

TOUCHDOWN WOLVERINES!@UMichFootball takes the lead over No. 4 UCLA

(via CBS) pic.twitter.com/TwgA12UeBq
— FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) November 21, 2026

Offensive Line – C-

Michigan’s offensive line was better than it looked in either of its last two games, although that isn’t saying that much. They helped pave the way for 120 yards in the run game, but didn’t do all that good a job of protecting Bryce Underwood in the passing game, allowing UCLA to get home with four sacks and two quarterback hurries. We’ll give the offensive line some credit for the strength of the opponent, but we’ll still need to see better if Michigan hopes to pull off the upset next week.

Defensive Line – A

Michigan’s defense was incredible on Saturday against the Bruins, and the defensive line was most responsible for the win. John Henry Daley was particularly disruptive on Senior Day with two sacks and a forced fumble, which was recovered by Dom Nichols near midfield. Tariq Boney and Jonah Lea’ea also had tackles for a loss.

The Wolverines also did a really good job against UCLA’s ground game, the strength of its offense, limiting the Bruins to just 107 rushing yards. The defense will need to be stout again next week, and a dominant effort up front is a great place to start.

Linebacker – B

Michigan’s linebackers also got in on the havoc, getting to UCLA’s backfield regularly and doing their part with the defensive line to stifle the run game. Troy Bowles led the group with nine tackles, including a big stop on fourth-and-short,t late in the fourth quarter. Nathaniel Staehling had six tackles, while Chase Taylor also had four. Taylor made some big plays in the game, bouncing back from a rough outing against Oregon last week.

If there’s an area to nitpick, the linebackers didn’t do the best job in coverage, with UCLA’s running backs being able to find some success in the screen game, something that’s been an issue all year.

Defensive Backs – B-

The defensive backs didn’t have to do much in this game, with UCLA’s wide receivers not posing much of a threat and quarterback Ty Dieffenbach misfiring on several throws. For the most part, the group did a good job of limiting big plays, save for the final drive of the game for UCLA, on which the Bruins were able to go the length of the field to tie the game – reminiscent of the loss to Iowa earlier in the year.

If there was a standout, it was safety Chris Bracy, who continued his dominance with 12 tackles and also had a key interception to stall a UCLA drive in the first quarter. He’s been Michigan’s best player for about a month now, and he’ll need to save his best performance for next week against the Buckeyes.

Special Teams – A-

Michigan’s special teams have been pretty subpar for much of the season, but they played a big role in the win over UCLA, namely kicker Jacob Baggett, who went 3-for-3 on his field goal attempts on Saturday, including a 52-yarder in overtime, which kept Michigan alive and gave the Wolverines a chance to win a few plays later. Michigan’s kicking game had been rather suspect for the last several weeks, but Baggett likely has cemented the job as the starter going forward.

The lone blemish for the special teams on Saturday was a muff from Salesi Moa, but he was able to recover it and prevent a disaster.

Jacob Baggett is clutch from 52 yards out. pic.twitter.com/4EMbxpaah5
— CBS Sports College Football 🏈 (@CBSSportsCFB) November 22, 2026

Coaching Staff – B+

Here’s a look at what the coaching staff did this week:

It wasn’t exactly a perfect game plan against UCLA, but Michigan did look much more inspired playing in front of the home crowd for one last time this season and with a top-5 team coming in. And perhaps a bit more inspired with Kyle Whittingham’s job on the line. There were still some questionable decisions early, namely a decision to punt on 4th-and-2 inside UCLA territory, right after attempting a deep pass on the play prior, but Michigan still looked the best it has in a while, so we’ll give the coaching staff some props today.

michigan.headline: Michigan Football stuns unbeaten No. 4 UCLA in triple OT
michigan.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 21: Bryce Underwood #19 of the Michigan Wolverines runs the ball during the first half against Anthony Sacca #39 of the UCLA Bruins at Michigan Stadium on November 21, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Jaime Crawford/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Michigan Wolverines stunned the previously undefeated No. 4 UCLA Bruins 18-16 in triple overtime on Saturday. It’s been a tumultuous season, but the Wolverines found a way to end UCLA’s unbeaten season in an unforgettable finish.

Here’s the recap, highlights and stats.

First quarter

Michigan opened its first possession with a bang as running back Savion Hiter sprinted 24 yards to pick up a first down. However, the drive ended as quarterback Bryce Underwood couldn’t connect with wide receiver Travis Johnson on third down.

On the defensive side, the Wolverines came to play on UCLA’s opening drive. The Bruins were forced to punt after Michigan safety Rod Moore came up with one of the biggest hits of his career – flattening UCLA running back Wayne Knight.

Rod Moore Jr. making his presence known. pic.twitter.com/yyd6c2j6bu
— CBS Sports (@CBSSports) November 21, 2026

Following an unsuccessful fourth down attempt for the Wolverines, UCLA regained possession at midfield. It didn’t take very long for Michigan to get the ball back though as safety Chris Bracy came down with his second interception of the year.

PICKED BY CHRIS BRACY. pic.twitter.com/eZ3hDFmEWI
— CBS Sports (@CBSSports) November 21, 2026

On the ensuing drive, the Wolverines showed life on offense. Underwood picked up a fist down on the ground and found tight end Mason Bonner for 15 yards. Michigan couldn’t pay it off though, eventually turning it over on downs again.

Second quarter

The Wolverines found a bit of success on the first possession of the second quarter as well. Underwood found Johnson for 19 yards and Bonner for 26 yards to get the ball to midfield, but UCLA eventually sacked Underwood and forced a punt.

Even though the offense remained scoreless, Michigan continued to shut down UCLA as defensive tackle Enow Etta had a sack on third down. On the ensuing punt, Salesi Moa returned it 23 yards to set Michigan up with great field position.

Sacked by Enow Etta! pic.twitter.com/x3HJgxGAMg
— Michigan Football (@UMichFootball) November 21, 2026

Michigan got into field goal range as Underwood found tight end Deakon Tonielli for a 17-yard gain and a first down. The Wolverines got on the scoreboard as kicker Jacob Baggett hit a 46-yard field goal to go up 3-0 with 3:08 to go in the half.

Michigan strikes first vs. No. 4 UCLA 🙌

Watch on CBS pic.twitter.com/AcxQeKGywt
— Big Ten Football (@B1Gfootball) November 21, 2026

In the final minutes of the half, the teams traded turnovers as Michigan edge rusher John Henry Daley forced a fumble, but Underwood gave it right back with a fumble himself. UCLA proceeded to hit a field goal to tie it 3-3 heading into halftime.

John Henry Daley doing John Henry Daley things 🔥

Michigan has the 3-0 lead and the ball in No. 4 UCLA territory.

Watch on CBS pic.twitter.com/eETPw9sE2x
— Big Ten Network (@BigTenNetwork) November 21, 2026

HALFTIME: Michigan 3, UCLA 3

Third quarter

On the first possession of the second half, Michigan’s defense came out on a mission. Daley continued his impressive outing with a sack and a tackle for loss on back to back plays, and cornerback Jyaire Hill had a tackle to force UCLA to punt.

The Wolverines were hoping to take a lead and it looked like that might be the case after Moa had two straight catches for a first down, and Hiter had a 14-yard run to get to midfield. However, Michigan eventually had to punt as the drive stalled.

On the following possession, UCLA used a fake punt to catch the Wolverines off guard and pick up a 27-yard gain. Michigan’s defense responded though, forcing a turnover on downs as linebacker Troy Bowles had a big fourth down tackle.

The Wolverines say NO on 4th down! pic.twitter.com/3nxVd8n9xA
— CBS Sports (@CBSSports) November 21, 2026

The Wolverines continued to seize momentum as UCLA fumbled it in the final seconds of the third quarter and allowed Michigan to take over in the red zone. On the final snap of the quarter, Hiter ran five yards to get Michigan to the 10-yard line.

@GeneSteratore breaks down the fumble call and why he agrees with it.

Michigan takes over deep in UCLA territory. pic.twitter.com/vtfGqOiIEs
— CBS Sports College Football 🏈 (@CBSSportsCFB) November 21, 2026

Fourth quarter

Just moments later, Underwood found Bonner for a 6-yard touchdown to take a 10-3 lead with 12:55 left in the game. Bonner continued his breakout performance with his third reception of the game and the first touchdown catch of his career.

Michigan is back on top 〽️

The Wolverines lead No. 4 UCLA 10-3 in the fourth quarter.

Watch on CBS pic.twitter.com/vAWgCoXrxo
— Big Ten Football (@B1Gfootball) November 21, 2026

Just moments later, Underwood found Bonner for a 6-yard touchdown to take a 10-3 lead with 12:55 left in the game. Bonner continued his breakout performance with his third reception of the game and the first touchdown catch of his career.

With just 5:24 to go in the game, UCLA regained possession with an opportunity to put together a game-tying drive. The Bruins pulled out all the stops to tie it, scoring a jump-pass touchdown with just 10 seconds remaining to force overtime.

Jump pass to tie the score 👀

No. 4 UCLA ties things up in the final seconds at Michigan.

Watch on CBS pic.twitter.com/m2h8ZQMO3K
— Big Ten Network (@BigTenNetwork) November 21, 2026

Overtime

Following an injury to quarterback Ty Dieffenbach on the first play of OT, UCLA settled for a field goal to go up 13-10. Michigan responded with a field goal of their own as Baggett kicked it in from 29 yards out to extend it to double overtime.

The Wolverines still couldn’t find the end zone, but Baggett drilled a clutch 52-yard field goal to regain a 16-13 lead. Michigan answered the bell on defense as well, holding UCLA to a field goal attempt as the Bruins forced a triple overtime.

Jacob Baggett is clutch from 52 yards out. pic.twitter.com/4EMbxpaah5
— CBS Sports College Football 🏈 (@CBSSportsCFB) November 22, 2026

In the third overtime period, Michigan took the lead, and this time for good. Underwood rolled out and found tight end Jalen Hoffman in the end zone for a game-winning score. Somehow, Michigan came out with an 18-16 triple overtime win.

Wolverines win it in 3OT 👀 pic.twitter.com/EfYmupDKRU
— Big Ten Network (@BigTenNetwork) November 22, 2026

FINAL SCORE: Michigan 18, UCLA 16

Michigan stat leaders

QB Bryce Underwood: 11-for-24, 127 passing yards, 1 touchdown

RB Savion Hiter: 26 carries, 104 rushing yards (career-high)

TE Mason Bonner: 3 catches, 47 receiving yards (career-high), 1 touchdown

DB Chris Bracy: 12 total tackles, 1 interception

DB Jyaire Hill: 6 total tackles, 1 tackle for loss, 1 pass deflection

UCLA stat leaders

QB Ty Dieffenbach: 19-for-30, 188 passing yards, 1 interception

RB Wayne Knight: 11 carries, 6 catches, 68 total yards

WR Semaj Morgan: 4 catches, 37 receiving yards

DB Malik Hartford: 9 total tackles, 1.5 tackles for loss

LB Donavyn Pellot: 8 total tackles, 1.5 tackles for loss

Up next

Michigan will look to finish the regular season on a high note against the rival Ohio State Buckeyes on Saturday.

msu.headline: Instant Recap: Michigan State gets stomped by Oregon
msu.body:
Michigan State’s Derrick Simmons, left, tackles Oregon’s Da'Jaun Riggs during the first quarter on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026 in East Lansing. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Whew, boy. That was the worst loss of the season.

It was all Oregon tonight. Michigan State’s offense struggled early, and Oregon scored halfway through the first quarter to give the Ducks a 7-0 lead behind a Brandon Smith 5-yard touchdown run.

Frederick Moore had a nice one-handed snag right before the second quarter started, but Liam Boyd would miss a 47-yard field goal for Michigan State’s first chance to put points on the board. The offense was starting to look solid behind Kayd Coffman’s play, but he would trip while running out of the pocket to turn the ball over on a 4th-and-3 from Oregon’s 28-yard line.

The defense did their best to keep the Spartans close, but their special teams did not. Chrishon McCray would muff the next punt by the Ducks to allow Oregon to take over in the redzone. The defense held tough and forced them to kick a field goal, and it made it a 10-0 game. Near the end of the first half, Dan Lanning called a fake field goal where the Ducks’ kicker was able to run it in from 15 yards out to give Oregon a 17-0 lead heading into halftime.

Once that fake field goal scored, it felt like the game was already out of reach.

Oregon opened up the second half with another touchdown run, this time from Simeon Price, to put them up 24-0.  Michigan State would respond with a touchdown of their own with a direct snap from the 1-yard line by Jaz Patterson, though it would be the only points they scored all night.

Both Brandon Smith and Simeon Price would add another touchdown run each for the Ducks, and Dylan Raiola found Dakorien Moore for a nice one-handed touchdown pass as Oregon continued to pile on the points. Oregon would go on to win 45 to 7. Michigan State moves to 3-8

Kayd Coffman completed 10 of his 19 passes for 106 yards and one interception. Jaz Patterson handled 16 carries, but only managed 26 yards. Brandon Tullis added 25 yards on eight carries. The Spartans’ leading receiver was Fredrick Moore with 31 yards on two catches.

It was a brutal loss, and one of those games where you wish it could’ve ended by the end of the third quarter, as Oregon kept putting more and more points on the scoreboard. Luckily for the Spartans, it’s not the end of the season, and they’ll finish it off with a matchup at Rutgers on Thanksgiving weekend. Let’s hope they can finish the season with a win.

Go Green!

Spartan hockey has gotten a bit spoiled in the last few years. Very solid teams, deep teams, and veteran leadership all helping MSU to an extremely successful yet slightly disappointing three-year run. This year, MSU is off to a slow start, and having just been swept by ND in their B1G opener, they look to regroup against their rivals and top team in the country. The ultimate question remains, what is wrong? With a team loaded with NHL talent, why does MSU look unlike themselves? We are going to dive in and see if we can figure it out.

We all knew heading into this season that this was going to be a young and inexperienced team. Talent is there, but experience is important. There are still some veterans on the team but not the number that have been in previous seasons and the experiences those veterans had in good times and bad went a long way. This team is very much still working on its chemistry and it takes time, but hopefully, that time comes soon.

One of the main concerns is the offensive struggles. This is something Nightingale has spoken on and is trying to fix. The team started off in exhibition and opening weekend finding the back of the net 4-6 times a night. Since then, the offense is struggling and in turn the record shows it. Puck movement has been lackluster and that may very well be a chemistry thing in knowing when a teammate is going to be somewhere before they are there. The Spartans have also struggled in taking the zone and stretch passes from the defense are basically nonexistent. Former MSU defenders like Matt Basgall were fantastic at the stretch pass and giving forwards quick opportunities in open ice. It is a skill set still under development with the current roster. MSU is getting stuck between the blue lines and unable to create real scoring chances at the level of years past. Nightingale said recently they need to create more offense by getting to the difficult areas of the ice. They need to get quicker and be scrappier in those areas to control the puck to open up possibilities for passes and one timers.

Goaltending has actually been quite good. The highly touted freshman Joshua Ravensbergen has been solid. His weakness has been shutting down the power play. That leads into another area that can be cleaned up and that is playing more disciplined. Staying out of the box, especially in crucial times in games is an element that can and should be cleaned up soon. This weekend against the weasels will be a good test. They will be bated into scrums, and they will need to stay out of the box to avoid the opponent’s hot power play and potent offense.

Every young team experiences growing pains. It is one reason why the NHL Draft model is something other sports should look at. The benefit of drafting a player and having them work out their kinks at the college level is very good developmentally for the players. With all the NHL talent on MSU, we are seeing first hand the need to develop their games. Ryker Lee has yet to get hot. He’s second on the team in points but he’s struggled to find the back of the net this season. With back to back years of Howard and Stramel’s goal scoring, we are feeling the drop in that star shooter. Romani has been the closest to taking that role and will hopefully catch fire soon.

MSU has been in the top 3 the last few years and had 1-seeds in the tourney only to get bumped early. Maybe some regular season bumps and the work to find the chemistry will strike at the right time. You just have to make the tourney; once there, it is anybody’s game. I wouldn’t count this team out yet, not with its talent and coaching staff. A sweep this weekend would be amazing but even a split would give this team some swagger back and perhaps get them trending in the right direction. Early season punches like the ND series can be useful if you grow from them. The showing this weekend will give us all a good idea of what the rest of the season will be like.

msu.headline: Getting To Know The Enemy: 6Qs About The Oregon Ducks
msu.body:
EUGENE, OR - NOVEMBER 14: Dylan Raiola #8 of the Oregon Ducks stands in the backfield during the 1st half of a game between the Michigan Wolverines and Oregon Ducks at Autzen Stadium on November 14, 2026 in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Al Sermeno/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images

Happy Thursday, TOC Nation. Our Michigan State Spartans Football Team are officially out of bowl contention.  But tomorrow night is Senior Night and we still want to show our support for the team before the lights at Spartan Stadium are shut off for the year.  I sat down with Thomas Cicansky from Addicted To Quack for a little Q&A.  Let’s see what he had to say.

The Only Colors: Oregon was #2 in the preseason poll.  At the time, were you a believer in that ranking?  Did you see the Ducks as a contender for the national championship?  Without foreseeing a major injury (i.e. Dante Moore), what was the floor for this team?

Thomas Cicansky:  Before the season I was 100% a believer in the Ducks and their ranking. The 3 previous
years coming into this season the Ducks:

Recruited at a Top 5 level out of high school and the portal

Finished in the top 6 of the final AP poll

On top of that, a ton of the team that made it to the semifinals in 2025 was returning for 2026 including a QB that turned down being a 1st round draft pick. I was fully bought into this potentially being the year for Oregon and the absolute floor was 9-3. Which as we sit here today is now the best-case scenario so that is a pretty good way to sum up how this season has gone relative to preseason expectations.

TOC: Oregon got by Boise State in the opener and then fell to Oklahoma State in week 2.  What did you learn about your team from those 2 games?

TC: I learned a lot as my expectations were sky high and the team was not even coming close to living up to those expectations. I’ll provide the most critical thing I learned about the team on each side of the ball.
Offense
I learned our O-Line coach, Alique Terry, had essentially been running a Ponzi scheme with his unit since being hired for the 2023 season and this year was the year the funds dried up. If your readers like, I can recount the entire story with this unit since his hiring in the comments if anyone is interested. But the short version is his first 3 seasons he was able to get by with players he inherited and transfers. But 2026 was going to be the
test of him as a developer with highly recruited O-Linemen and the first two weeks it was a complete and utter failure. The O-Line couldn’t move Boise State or Oklahoma State in the run game and was routinely letting pressure get home against 3-man rushes. They were just physically overwhelmed by teams they absolutely shouldn’t have been overwhelmed by.
They improved physically since the UCLA game, but there are still lots of assignment errors and poor technique that very much limit Oregon’s rushing attack.
Defense
This defense, while talented, was making a lot of mental errors and our new coordinator was blitzing too much. Luckily this has been cleaned up a lot from the first two weeks of the season, but the defense is still good for about 1 goofball play per game that allows a super explosive play.

TOC: QB Dante Moore suffered that nasty head injury in game 4 and is out for the year.  Dylan Raiola, who was the starter at Nebraska the last 2 seasons and was the #1 QB in the 2024 cycle, has taken over.  How is he different from Moore?  What are his strengths and weaknesses?

TC: It’s interesting you framed your question this way because the biggest and most relevant difference between Moore and Raiola might be both Raiola’s greatest strength and greatest weakness.
The major difference between the two are their mechanics. Dante Moore might have the cleanest mechanics and throwing motion I have literally ever seen and it’s why he still might be a first-round pick despite hardly playing this year.
Meanwhile, Dylan Raiola, when faced with an ounce of pressure, doesn’t step into his throws and fully relies upon his upper body. The internet thinks it’s because Patrick Mahomes is his idol, but the real reason is Raiola played catcher in baseball growing up and so from his amateur sporting career, he was used to making throws from his knees or throws that are entirely dependent on the upper body.
This is probably his greatest strength because when the pocket has completely collapsed, he can still get off a bomb downfield without having to step into his throw. The game winning touchdown against USC and the first touchdown against Michigan are great examples of this.

However, this also can get Raiola into trouble sometimes because he isn’t planting and throwing with a strong lower half so these balls tend to float into the secondary. When a receiver isn’t wide open the ball hangs up in dangerous space. His 2nd pick against UCLA is a memorable example of this.

TOC: Give us one name on offense and one on defense that MSU fans are certain to hear a lot of on Friday night.  What makes those guys so good?

TC: Offense
Dierre Hill Jr. is the lightning to Jordon Davison’s thunder in Oregon’s backfield. Davison has been hurt the last two and half weeks meaning Dierre has needed to be both Thunder and Lightning and he is more than capable of being a bell cow running back when called upon. Davison might be back this week, but if he isn’t, Dierre will get a lot of work and when Dierre Hits 6th gear, it’s special.
Defense
Matayo Uiagalelei is an incredibly well-rounded defensive end/OLB. He doesn’t have elite quick twitch pass rushing ability, but he can bull rush or use speed when rushing the passer and has been setting a great edge in the run game this year. Oregon’s other 4th year defensive end/OLB Teitum Tuitoti suffered a season ending injury at the end of the Ohio State game so the end opposite Matayo was filled by committee last week against Michigan. Uiagalelei hardly left the field and I expect will hardly leave the field Friday.

TOC: Oregon is favored by 15.5 points over on FanDuel.  What would it take for Michigan State to come out on top?

TC: If your readers are confused why Oregon lost to Oklahoma State and Illinois but have beat USC and Ohio State by 2 TDs, it’s actually a very simple explanation and it’s how Michigan State has a legitimate shot in this game despite the point spread. It all comes back to that offensive line I was lamenting earlier. That unit is incredibly inconsistent meaning Oregon has this all or nothing inconsistent offence.  Any given game they are capable of scoring 40+ or being held to less than 17. If defenses make mistakes or can’t cover for 2 seconds Oregon can light it up with explosive passing plays. But if defenses are disciplined and have a plan for keeping
everything in front of them, Oregon can’t counter and efficiently march down the field.
I think that’s Michigan State’s path to victory. Keep everything in front of them, force Oregon to have to try to march the field, and on third and long maybe Anelu Lafaele can create some pressure that forces Raiola into turning the ball over to spark the Spartan offense.

TOC: Predict the final score.

TC: From afar, I’ve been impressed with Michigan State’s defense this year and I think Joe Rossi will understand the assignment for the best way to slow down Oregon. On a short week travelling 3 time zones, I think the max amount Oregon will score is 31 but probably closer to 27-24ish.
But the problem I foresee for the Spartans is the other side of the ball. This Oregon defense has really improved over the course of the season and has done so against strong offenses. Provided Oregon takes care of the ball and makes Michigan State have to go 65+ yards each drive, I feel pretty confident Oregon can hold Michigan State to 13 or less.
I think I’ll settle on 24-10 Oregon.
I’ve learned to expect the unexpected with the 2026 Oregon Ducks so definitely not taking the win for granted.

TOC: Aside from former athletes (that includes Phil Knight since he was on the track & field team), who is Oregon’s most famous alum?

TC: This is tough because Oregon is an athletic school. We take a ton of pride in our Track, Diamond sports, and basketball. But excluding athletes, the first that came to my mind is actor Ty Burell, who played the best character on Modern Family, Phil Dunphy. But other famous actors as well include Kaitlin Olson and Sam Elliot.

tigers.headline: Assessing the Tigers payroll in the wake of Troy Melton’s extension
tigers.body:
Detroit Tigers CEO and Chairman Chris Ilitch, manager A.J. Hinch and President of Baseball Operations Scott Harris and talk during Spring Training Tuesday, February 21, 2023. Tigers9 022123 Kd3999 | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

While the deal isn’t fully official until the medicals are completed, the Detroit Tigers have come to terms with right-handed starting pitcher Troy Melton on a long-term extension offer. The deal reportedly guarantees Melton six years and $46.5 million, with incentives and a club option for the 2033 season that could take the contract to a total of $80 million over seven years.

This is a pretty smart decision from both the Tigers and the 25-year-old Melton. Our thoughts quickly turned to potential extensions for talented youngsters like Jackson Jobe and Max Clark. The club already has AL Rookie of the Year Kevin McGonigle, as well as infielder Colt Keith signed to long-term extensions. It will be interesting to see if the Tigers pursue extensions with their other talented young players prior to the December 1 lockout of the players by MLB owners. They don’t want to get stuck with too much guaranteed money on the books for the long haul, but at the same time these contracts are certainly very team friendly as long as the players involved produce as expected.

Our next thought was how this sets up the Tigers payroll for 2027. The Tigers entered the 2026 season with a payroll that was pushing towards the $244 million luxury tax threshold. However, after trading away three of their most expensive players in Tarik Skubal, Casey Mize, and Jake Rogers, all of whom were in their final year of arbitration eligibility prior to free agency, the final estimated Tigers payroll for 2026 came down to $195 million according to FanGraphs.

FanGraphs’ Roster Resource now estimates the Tigers’ 2027 Opening Day payroll at $169 million in the wake of Melton’s extension. That total would’ve put the Tigers 15th most in payroll in the major leagues in 2026, right in the middle. These are the salaries for their free agent deals and extensions on the books for 2027.

Framber Valdez – $47.5M

Javier Báez – $24M

Emilio Pagán – $11.5M

Kyle Finnegan – $10M

Drew Anderson – $8M

Troy Melton – $7.75M

Colt Keith – $4.77M

Kevin McGonigle – $2.75M

Jacob Waguespack – $1.3M

In addition, the Tigers do have a few arbitration eligible players estimated to make over $5 million in 2027. Riley Greene is estimated to earn $9.3 million, while Spencer Torkelson is estimated at $7.7 million for the 2027 season. Those two players are under team control for 2027-2028, and will then be free agents in 2029.

Zach McKinstry is estimated to make $5 million next season, while both Will Vest and Kerry Carpenter are estimated to make $4.4 million and $4.1 million, respectively.

So, looking forward to the rest of the offseason, the Tigers are still in fine shape to go make a big signing or just continue to build up their pitching staff and possibly hunt for a better bat in a part-time role. Ihey were willing to spend something like $240 million in 2026. That doesn’t mean they’re planning on keeping payroll that high year after year, but it seems likely they could add another $30-40 million in payroll this offseason and still be well short of their 2026 Opening Day payroll projection.

There’s room to spend. It’s more a question of a lack of major impact players that fit this offseason. Presumably there’s also some trepidation about signing any big free agent deals with so much up in the air this offseason. With the CBA negotiations and lockout coming, most teams would prefer certainty as to what the sports rules and payrolls are going to look like under the next CBA before making any huge commitments. Some teams will obviously make exceptions for Tarik Skubal and a handful of other top free agents, but the Tigers don’t seem like they’re going to be involved with those players.

Still it’s interesting to consider the Tigers payroll situation in light of the possibility that the owners do get their way and there’s a cap and floor instituted for 2028 as proposed. Under the owners’ most recent proposal, the floor would be $180.2 million against a hard cap of $258.2 million. Part of that would involve smaller market teams like the Tigers getting more in revenue sharing money, but actually being required to spend up to that $180.2 million level. Since the Tigers were willing to spend roughly $240 million for the 2026 season, with additional league revenue coming in they would likely be in a position to spend close to that level on a yearly basis going forward.

The Tigers have their second biggest annual salary coming off the books after 2027 as Javier Báez reaches free agency. That takes $24 million off the payroll heading into 2028. And, should Framber Valdez bounce back in year two in Detroit with a good season, there’s a fair chance he would choose to decline his 2028 player option with the Tigers, worth $35 million, and head back to free agency. A cap and floor system might have some impact on Valdez’s desire to return to free agency a year early as well. Even so, while the Tigers’ expenses will increase elsewhere as players get raises and then reach arbitration, there is plenty of money bound to come off the books in the next few seasons as well.

Obviously, this is speculative as there’s nothing to suggest the players are going to give the owners what they want in the CBA negotiations. Still, thinking through the general possibilities shows the Tigers in pretty good shape going forward whether a cap and floor system is put in place or not. They could clearly afford even a $400 million offer to Tarik Skubal if they thought that was the best way to allocate their payroll. With several talented younger players already locked up on long-term deals, minimal major commitments to older players, and with a still good farm system brewing up more major league talent to come, the Tigers future looks pretty bright if the front office can finally make the right moves to put them seriously into contention on a yearly basis.

tigers.headline: Tigers sign RHP Troy Melton to a six-year extension
tigers.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Troy Melton #52 of the Detroit Tigers delivers a pitch against the Chicago White Sox at Rate Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Jayden Mack/Getty Images) | Getty Images

While we were waiting for non-tender deadline news, and there was none involving the Tigers, who tendered contracts to all eligible players other than Matt Vierling, who was already DFA’d on Tuesday, the club had other business instead. Multiple reports emerged on Friday evening that the Tigers have inked right-hander Troy Melton to a six-year contract extension that guarantees him $46.5 million with incentives and a club option for 2033 that could max out at $80 million over seven years. The deal is still pending a physical and not officially announced yet.

The hard-throwing right-hander will turn 26 years old in about two weeks. He has one year and 68 days of MLB service time currently, so this deal arrives as Melton was still five full seasons from free agency. Exchanging an extra year until he’ll reach free agency, and potentially two years if the Tigers use their club option, to guarantee himself at least $46.5 million is a pretty good deal for both sides. Melton wouldn’t have reached free agency until he was headed into his age 31 season, and with pitcher injuries being what they are, there’s always the risk that he wouldn’t be as valuable by that point in his career.

From the Tigers’ perspective, they locked up six years of Melton at less than eight million a season, a bargain for a pitcher who is on track to be worth roughly 2 WAR per season if he continues on his current track. Of course, the Tigers, and no doubt Melton himself, expect continued improvements in the years ahead. There are plenty of incentives that could make the deal much more lucrative for Melton, but if he earns them the Tigers won’t have any problem paying him extra. With a 96-97 mph fastball with big extension that can reach triple digits, along with a deep and developing arsenal of pitches including a sinker, cutter, slider, curveball, and splitter, the potential here is pretty enormous. Melton just hasn’t found the strikeout touch consistently to take him into the upper tiers of starting pitchers around the league quite yet.

2026 was Melton’s first full season as a major leaguer after debuting in the second half of 2025 in a mixed role that included starts and high leverage relief appearances, and some good performances in the postseason. This season didn’t get off to a good start as Melton had some elbow inflammation in spring camp. The Tigers shut him down and took their time, getting him back on the mound in late May.

Melton went on to make 20 starts totaling 114.1 innings pitched. He posted a 2.76 ERA and a 4.09 FIP over that span. He keeps balanced splits, leaning on that deep repertoire of pitches. With more consistency from his good slider-split combination, he should be able to strike out more hitters. For now, the fact that he attacks the zone aggressively and doesn’t issue many walks, while controlling contact, is a great foundation to build on going forward.

His season didn’t end well, as his performance fell off in late August and into September. Eventually he was shut down after a start on September 20 with forearm tightness and general arm fatigue. Reports have since emerged that he’d avoided any serious injury. The Tigers must be pretty convinced in his medicals to have extended the extension offer, and perhaps those issues during the season convinced Melton that it was a good idea to come to an agreement and guarantee himself the money now.

One also wonders what this says about the status of Jackson Jobe and Max Clark, two other highly talented youngsters who have shown some nice flashes in the major leagues but are really just getting started. It will be interesting to see if this is just the first in a flurry of extensions designed to provide stability and cost certainty with the Tigers top young players just as the sport heads into an extremely uncertain time with the lockout and CBA negotiations looming.

tigers.headline: A final look at the Detroit Tigers non-tender candidates
tigers.body:
Detroit Tigers president of baseball operations Scott Harris watches practice during spring training at TigerTown in Lakeland, Fla. on Friday, Feb. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Friday, November 20 is the non-tender deadline for all arbitration eligible players. By 5:00 p.m. ET, every pre-arbitration and arbitration eligible player must be tendered a contract by their respective teams. Arb eligible players may ultimately turn down the offer and renegotiate or go to an arbitration hearing, typically in February though who knows this year, to decide their 2027 salary, but teams must tender them a contract by the deadline or they immediately become free agents without having to go through waivers. Typically, avoiding waivers is what non-tenders are for, allowing teams to try and negotiate a minor league deal rather than simply designating the player for assignment and giving the rest of the league a crack at them.

Often, players who aren’t going to be tendered a contract are just designated for assignment at the deadline to finalize the 40-man roster in advance of December’s Rule 5 draft. That deadline passed on Tuesday, and saw the Tigers trade infield prospect Jace Jung to the Los Angeles Angels for cash considerations to open one spot. Shortstop Trey Sweeney, outfielder Matt Vierling, and left-handed pitching prospect Jake Miller were all DFA’d off the 40-man roster as well. They’ll be non-tendered in the meantime. Free agent acquisition Emilio Pagán, along with prospects Josue Briceño, Max Anderson, and Peyton Graham were all added to the 40-man roster at that point, and the roster now stands at 40 players.

Here are the Tigers arbitration eligible players for 2027, their ages and service time, along with their 2026 salary and finally MLB Trade Rumors arbitration estimates.

Will Vest- Age 31 (5.100 years): $3.950MM —>$4.4MM

Zach McKinstry- Age 31 (5.099 years): $4.2MM —> $5MM

Riley Greene- Age 26 (4.110 years): $5.0MM —>$9.3MM

Spencer Torkelson- Age 27 (4.076 years): $4.075MM —>$7.7M

Kerry Carpenter-Age 29 (4.057 years): $3.275MM —>$4.1MM

Tyler Holton- Age 30 (4.047 years): $1.575MM —>$2.4MM

Beau Brieske- Age 28 (4.007 years): $1.157MM —>$1.5MM

Reese Olson- Age 27 (3.123 years): $818,100 —>$1.5MM

Wenceel Pérez- Age 26 (3.000 years): $803,400 —>$1.4 MM

Parker Meadows- Age 26 (2.169 years): $805,300 —>$1MM

Teams that weren’t going to offer their arbitration eligible players a contract often genearlly, but not always, would have just DFA’d them back on Tuesday to clear space for their additions. On the other hand, waiting does give a few extra days to look through the newly available players for potential upgrades, or to perhaps work out a trade of their own arbitration eligible player instead of just releasing the player outright. Typically this involves a veteran player who underperformed but still has value, but is also due a sizable raise in arbitration. The Tigers don’t really a player who fits that description, though Spencer Torkelson is arguably in that camp, so expect Friday to be pretty quiet unless they’re actively working to trade away one of the players above. Sweeney and Vierling haven’t been claimed as of yet, and so the Tigers will have them on their non-tender list, but they probably won’t have much company.

We’ve wondered if the Tigers might try to deal someone like Spencer Torkelson or Kerry Carpenter for minor league pitching depth as they get a bit more expensive, but there’s nothing to suggest that a trade is coming and both players value is at a low point. Neither is making that much, though Torkelson’s projected $7.7 million is starting to get a little close to his actual projected value for 2027. However, Scott Harris has continued to speak highly of Torkelson as a piece of the Tigers’ offense, so we’ll assume he’ll be tendered a contract.

Carpenter is still going to be quite cheap, although his status after the past two seasons is pretty uncertain. The injury history and declining recent production makes it unlikely that many teams will be inquiring about the 29-year-old outfielder, though his projected raise to $4.1 million is still quite inexpensive if he can get healthy and start turning things around at the plate. On the other hand, he’s a well liked player in the Tigers’ organization, and if teams aren’t offering anything in trade, non-tendering him would allow him to become a free agent and have some say in choosing his future home rather than exposing him to waivers via a DFA. The same could be true of fellow outfielders Wenceel Pérez and Parker Meadows, but that duo is still inexpensive and young enough that the Tigers will probably stick with them for now.

Utilityman Zach McKinstry isn’t projected for much of a raise, and his jack of all trades stylings help fill in gaps on the Tigers roster. Still, after a rough year at the plate he’s certainly a possible candidate to be non-tendered too, just as Andy Ibáñez was last year. It’s hard to imagine the Tigers managing to trade him for anything they need. Still, he could be tendered a contract to keep him under club control and then released later if the Tigers sign another free agent or claim a player off waivers before the season begins. At age 31, with minimal trade value, non-tendering him would at least allow him some control over his 2027 landing spot as well.

Finally, while the Tigers will keep Will Vest, right-hander Beau Brieske is out of options and is a pretty good non-tender candidate as well. The right-hander has spent the past two seasons dealing with shoulder issues. He briefly returned in May of 2026 but was roughed up. Still, he eventually got his legs under him and posted a 3.04 ERA and a 3.48 FIP from June 10 until the end of the season. With relief help at a premium, the Tigers might decide to keep him, but ideally they’d just non-tender him now and re-sign him to a minor league deal before the lockout begins. They could still pay him to accept this and stash him in Triple-A to begin the year. Of course, in that case Brieske could just choose to go elsewhere, but it’s not as though his services will be in high demand.

Last year the Tigers non-tendered Ibáñez and six pitchers, but the 40-man roster situation was pretty crowded due to pitcher injuries throughout the season. Tanner Rainey, Sean Guenther, Dugan Darnell, Jason Foley, Jack Little, and Tyler Mattison were all designated for assignment at the 40-man roster last year, and then ultimately non-tendered as well. Rainey, Little, and Mattison all ultimately accepted minor league deals with the Tigers.

The non-tender deadline is always the final Friday before Thanksgiving, per the 2022-2026 collective bargaining agreement. Generally, there isn’t a whole lot of big news, but occasionally a trade or two will go through in advance of the deadline, or there will be a surprise non-tender candidate. With the trade market perking up this week, there’s at least a chance that the Tigers make a small trade and non-tender a player or two to clear space for future free agent signings. Really the interest today is whether teams come to agreements with players quickly, and how the looming CBA fight might affect players’ willingness to actually sign a tendered contract now rather than waiting for an arbitration hearing under a new agreement.

tigers.headline: Detroit Tigers News: Silver Slugger, Tarik Skubal, Dustin May, Hall of Fame, MLB hot stove
tigers.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 27, 2026: Kevin McGonigle #7 of the Detroit Tigers bats during the seventh inning against the Pittsburgh Pirates at Comerica Park on September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by George Kubas/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images

Happy Wednesday, everyone! It took until late in the day yesterday for there to be much to report for the Tigers, but we do have a few bits of news. The Tigers netted an MLB-best three Silver Slugger Awards for Kevin McGonigle, Riley Greene, and Dillon Dingler, and they also cleared up some room on their roster with some moves. It’s also fun for some experts to debate whether or not Tarik Skubal might return to the Motor City (we know, we know). We’ve also got some general MLB updates, looking at some free agent signings, some rumors, and the newest Hall of Fame ballot.

Let’s get right into it!

Detroit Tigers News

The Tigers have made some moves during a very important week for the roster.

To make room on the 40-man roster, the following four players were designated for assignment: INF Jace Jung, LHP Jake Miller; INF Trey Sweeney; and OF Matt Vierling.
— Tigers PR (@DetroitTigersPR) November 17, 2026

The Tigers took home three Silver Slugger Awards this season, an MLB best, with awards going to Kevin McGonigle, Riley Greene, and Dillon Dingler.

The Tigers have three Silver Slugger winners: Dillon Dingler (C), Riley Greene (OF) and Kevin McGonigle (UTIL).

The three individual winners marks the most of any MLB team this year and ties 1987 (Nokes, Whitaker, Trammell) for the most in franchise history
— Cody Stavenhagen (@CodyStavenhagen) November 18, 2026

Could Tarik Skubal be a good fit to come back to the Tigers? While it’s highly unlikely given the offseason moves we’ve seen from the team over recent years, the folks at Sports Illustrated point out that there could be one very good reason for Skubal to come back to Detroit, citing his familiarity with the organization and the staff, as well as the players.

Another aspect that could play into Skubal’s free agency is any relationships he’s established with managers, coaches, teammates or front office personnel.

In that regard, a reunion with the Tigers could make sense for Skubal, as they’re still managed by A.J. Hinch, his skipper for the last six seasons. His longtime pitching coach, Chris Fetter, remains with the organization, too, as do many of his former teammates.

tigers.headline: Dillon Dingler, Kevin McGonigle, and Riley Greene win Silver Slugger awards
tigers.body:
Aug 15, 2025; Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA; Detroit Tigers catcher Dillon Dingler (13) and left fielder Riley Greene (31) celebrate the win over the Minnesota Twins at Target Field. Mandatory Credit: Bruce Kluckhohn-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Awards season is finally concluding for the 2026 season, and tonight the Silver Slugger awards were announced. The award recognizes the best offensive player at each position in both leagues, and the Tigers took home three of them on the night. Riley Greene won a Silver Slugger among AL outfielders, while Kevin McGonigle took home his first in the utility category. Catcher Dillon Dingler also took home his first Silver Slugger as the top hitting catcher in the American League.

The 26-year-old Greene took home his second straight Silver Slugger with a campaign that featured 21 homers in 140 games, with a slash line of .280/.370/.474 on the year. His 136 wRC+ was the highest of his career, and he was able to trim strikeouts and add walks from his 2025 production for a better all around performance at the plate. With two years remaining until free agency, questions have started to swirl around the Tigers long-term plans for Greene, but there has been no public acknowledgement of interest in an extension from either party. His status throughout 2027 will be interesting in that light, but Greene has established himself as one of the top slugging outfielders in the game even as his defensive performance has slipped each of the past two seasons.

As for Dingler, the 28-year-old catcher looked like a sure fire MVP candidate for much of his second full season in the major leagues. Already the best all-around defensive catcher in baseball, Dingler hit 27 home runs with a .243/.302/.446 slash line, good for a 107 wRC+ on the year. By the end of July, Dingler already had 23 home runs with a .269/.333/.520 slash line, good for a 136 wRC+, but between catching most games and DH-ing a lot due to the Tigers need for offense, he crashed to Earth in August and September. Hopefully the Tigers can get him off his feet a little more in 2027 and get something closer to that first half performance all season long.

As for McGonigle, not much needs be said. The AL Rookie of the Year put together one of the best campaigns from a 21-year-old in league history. He hit 18 home runs a posted a 129 wRC+ with a slash line of .278/.376/.430 on the year. He takes home the Silver Slugger in the utility category after splitting his time pretty equally between shortstop and third base, which is all the more impressive from a rookie trying to adapt to the big leagues.

No team racked up more Silver Slugger awards in either league this season. The last time the Detroit Tigers had three in a year was back in 1987, when Alan Trammell, Lou Whitaker, and Matt Nokes all won the award.

Congratulations to Riley Greene, Kevin McGonigle, and Dillon Dingler, your Tigers’ Silver Slugger award winners for 2026.
